subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make, and at the same time I make a request to hon. members of the house to grant unanimous consent for the presentation tomorrow of a resolution and also a bill respecting the British Columbia steamship services strike.
The government has had under continuous consideration the endeavour to achieve a settlement of the strike which has tied up the British Columbia coast steamship services of the Canadian Pacific Railway since May 16 of this year. The situation has assumed urgency, and I can tell the house that in the last few days every possibility of a settlement has been exhausted. All that remains is for legislative action to be taken to provide a solution to a situation which has proven so difficult for the people of British Columbia, and in particular for those living on Vancouver island and the northern areas of British Columbia, and which has had such an adverse effect generally on the economy.
Ever since negotiations commenced last September for renewal of the various collective agreements involved the facilities of the Department of Labour have been at the disposal of the parties, and every effort has been made by the department and by the Minister of Labour to effect a settlement by conciliation and negotiation. Effective June 1, 1958, the company signed collective agreements covering four groups of employees represented by the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks. Notwithstanding continued efforts by the department and the personal intervention of the Minister of Labour, it has not been possible to bring about any settlement between the company and the seafarers' international union, which had first taken strike action in May of this year. Meantime, on June 24 the two unions representing the officers had also notified the C.P.R. that they were declaring themselves on strike.
During most of the time the strike against the C.P.R. ships has been in effect some services in the coastal regions of British Columbia have been provided by the Black Ball ferries previously referred to. Since, however, the C.P.R. supplied the bulk of the services the Black Ball ships have been able to only partially fulfil the needs of the area, and increasing hardship and loss have been accruing to the residents of Vancouver island and other coastal points on the mainland of British Columbia. On Friday last the Black Ball ferry service was interrupted by strike action and conditions in the area reached a critical point, with certain essential supplies and services being almost entirely discontinued.
As I said a moment ago, every effort has been made to resolve the dispute by negotiation and also to have the parties renew negotiations on a voluntary basis. All these efforts have been unsuccessful, and for that reason other steps must now be taken. I am accordingly giving notice now of the intention to introduce legislation immediately to provide for the appointment of an administrator of the British Columbia coast steamship services for the resumption of operations and return to work under the administrator immediately after the legislation has passed, and for the continuation of operations under the administrator while the process of negotiation is resumed looking to a voluntary settlement. The powers of the administrator will continue until such time

Canadian Pacific Steamships as settlement is arrived at. A resolution has been drawn up and handed in and will appear in Votes and Proceedings tomorrow. That resolution will read as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the resumption of the British Columbia coast steamship service operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, including provisions for the appointment of an administrator to carry on all or any part of the said services, and for other related matters.
The bill will be printed and available for distribution tomorrow morning. The house will be asked-and that is the request I make under the circumstances-to give unanimous consent to taking up the resolution tomorrow, and as soon as it is adopted to proceed at once with consideration of the bill through all stages.
There was a tentative arrangement made that tomorrow the debate on external affairs would be proceeded with. However, in view of the present position, the adjournment without a set date on the part of the security council, I would suggest that the question to be considered could be postponed for another day and that this matter, so important to the economic life of the people of British Columbia, might receive the support of all hon. members in all parts of the house, to the end that without delay, following discussion, action may be taken to resolve, in so far as the people are concerned, a situation that is proving very difficult and trying and one of great discomfort, which in addition is causing severe damage to the tourist industry in that province.
If the house would agree I should be only too willing to fix any date as the day for the debate on external affairs. There is no indication that immediate action will be taken in New York, certainly not before the beginning of next week.
In making this request I do so because I believe it is of the essence that parliament be seized of this matter at once. We have made every effort and have met with no success. Indeed, there is no possibility of a settlement being arrived at which will make possible the resumption of the services unless parliament in its wisdom will act. I am not given to endeavouring to bring about changes in the legislative planning of the house or the planning of debates, but in this case I do make an appeal to hon. members to realize the situation that prevails and, to that end, make possible consideration tomorrow of this extremely important matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with interest and concern to what the Prime Minister has just said. The house will recall that only yesterday the hon. member for

Laurier and also the hon. member for Skeena asked questions with regard to the strike in British Columbia to which the Prime Minister has referred and the seriousness of which is apparent to us all. In replying to these questions only yesterday the Minister of Labour merely stated that-
-the government still has this matter under very serious consideration.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we would have been the more surprised, I think, at the announcement the Prime Minister has made so soon after these questions if we had not read in the press this morning the Canadian Press story-which is dated July 22-to the effect that-
Legislation for halting the west coast C.P.R. steamship tie-up will be brought before the federal cabinet tomorrow, it was learned late today.
Informants said it will involve passage of a back to work measure by parliament.
The situation, of course, Mr. Speaker, is serious, but I think we have to be equally serious as members of parliament about the way in which we approach this problem in order to resolve it. The Prime Minister has said that the strike began on May 16, 68 days ago, and the report of a conciliation board set up by the government to consider the strike was received, I believe, by the Minister of Labour on April 24. The matter has been before the government for a considerable time.
Some hon. members will recall that in 1950 parliament and the country were confronted with a grave transportation emergency owing to a railway strike which was national in scope, which if it had been allowed to continue would have had disastrous national results. This strike in British Columbia is equally serious in a sense for those who are directly concerned with it on Vancouver island and on the mainland, but it differs from the strike in 1950 in that that latter strike was national in scope as well as in character.
The house will no doubt recall that at that time in 1950 the prime minister of the day, almost within hours of the beginning of that strike, called parliament together in special session and introduced legislation to deal with that national emergency, as it undoubtedly was. At that time, on introduction of the legislation, the leader of the Conservative party quite rightly emphasized that even in an emergency there must be sufficient time for members of parliament to give consideration to the measure that was being introduced by the government. Mr. Drew said, as reported at page 3 of Hansard of August 29, 1950:
It is highly desirable that there be an opportunity for hon. members to examine the bill, and

that there be an explanation by the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), before hon. members are called upon to express an opinion upon the bill itself.
Later on Mr. Drew said, as reported at page 4 of Hansard:
I am certain that the bill will be dealt with much more expeditiously if we have it before us and have the explanation that will enable us to understand the intention of the government in presenting it.
If I remember right the prime minister of the day and the minister of labour did explain the purpose and nature of the action they were asking parliament to take, and the bill was before members who had an opportunity to consider it before debate took place. I suggest that the same procedure certainly should be adopted at this time. For that purpose and because we do not wish to delay the matter unduly, having regard to the right of parliament to give it adequate and informed consideration, I suggest that the Prime Minister should get unanimous consent at this time to introduce the resolution, that perhaps the resolution could be passed at once and the bill then printed and, as the Prime Minister has suggested, be distributed to members sometime tomorrow morning.
But I also suggest that we should not proceed to deal with it immediately in the afternoon, as there certainly would be very little opportunity to consider the bill, but that we should proceed to deal with it on Friday morning. This does not seem to me to represent unnecessary delay, and such a procedure would have the additional advantage of enabling us to proceed with the debate on external affairs which had been contemplated for tomorrow. While it may well be, as the Prime Minister has said, that the security council has adjourned and there will be no immediate decision taken in New York with respect to the Middle East situation, nevertheless that situation remains tense and dangerous, and I think the time has come when we should be given the opportunity in a full dress debate in parliament to state our views with regard to it.
I think the opposition, and it is quite right that it should, has attempted to be cooperative in this matter with regard to procedure. There have been very good reasons for postponing the debate and we have accepted them, but I would hope that the debate could go ahead tomorrow, because that would also give us a few extra hours to study the legislation that is to be brought forward. I think, as Mr. Drew thought in 1950 with respect to an emergency even greater in its nature, that the opportunity
Canadian Pacific Steamships to give the legislation that kind of study will not delay the bill more than a few hours and will ensure that all members of parliament can discuss it in an intelligent and informed way. I therefore make that suggestion to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of making a lengthy statement with respect to this matter, for I am sure all hon. members and the people of the country are aware of our sincere interest with respect to the situation on the west coast. With regard to agreeing to the introduction of the resolution and the bill without notice in order that the house may deal with the legislation at the earliest possible moment, we have no objection to that either. We regret, however, that it has taken the government such a long, long time to deal with the situation. We have kept a very close watch on developments over the past weeks, and know the hardships that have been caused the employees involved and the general public.
We feel that while the approach of arranging for an administrator to operate the steamship line may bring relief to some quarters, nevertheless it only deals with the immediate problem and can do relatively little to solve the longer range and more important aspects of coastal shipping. The government would have merited extreme commendation if it had dealt with coastal shipping problems some months ago. It would still receive accolades from all parts of the country if it would consider dealing with passenger and other shipping facilities from the point of view of providing a service to the general public and to our economy.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say just one word in connection with the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. What I was asking for was expedited action in order to meet the situation. In 1950, as I recall, there was no resolution. There was simply a bill introduced, and at the time the request was made by the then leader of the Conservative party there was no bill available. In the present case it is necessary to introduce a resolution. At the resolution stage the fullest information will be available so that, in so far as the bill itself is concerned, after discussion has taken place at the resolution stage the house and the country will have every bit of information that will be available on the bill.
I am, naturally, in the hands of the house. If the house does not give consent then of course 1 must proceed in the ordinary way. This may mean very well that we will not be in a position to act before the beginning of the week. After all, once the discussion

Canadian Pacific Steamships gets under way, if we started tomorrow and took even two days we would be able to get passage, if the bill is acceptable to the house, by Saturday. Then the legislation could be sent over to the other place, and if acceptable to the other place there could be a resumption of service by Saturday.
However, if the Leader of the Opposition takes the view he does, and does not feel like altering that view, I can only say that it may very well be that there may not be any legislation passed during the present week. Monday is private members' day. I simply point out these facts. If, however, unanimous consent is not forthcoming, then all we will be able to do is introduce the resolution and go no further.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGIS- LATION DEALING WITH STRIKE
speechtext:
May I add
one word to what has already been said by the Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister stated that he is anxious to expedite this legislation, and has made a suggestion upon which the Leader of the Opposition has commented. What I am saying now is in support of what the Leader of the Opposition has said, that we are willing to go even farther than the Prime Minister has asked by consenting to the passage of the resolution now. Once the resolution has passed we will then be in a position to have the bill before us and will be able to consider the bill on Thursday, at which time the debate on external affairs could take place.
Under those circumstances we could not, by any stretch of the imagination, be holding up the legislation at all. We are anxious to assist the passage of this legislation in view of the urgency to which the Prime Minister has referred. If the resolution is not passed until tomorrow, and we get the bill after the passage of the resolution, we will then be in the stage of committee of the whole and may not have, at that time, the opportunity to which I think the opposition is entitled, to consider the bill as we should.
In effect we are saying, upon the suggestion put before us by the Prime Minister, that we consent to the passage of the resolution at once so that we may have the bill before us and ascertain what the contents of the bill are. We are, we think, entitled to know what the powers of the administrator are going to be and what the terms of the resumption of service are. All these things must be given consideration, and it strikes me that if we had that information by getting the bill today we would then be in a position to ponder upon it until tomorrow and the bill would move much faster through the various stages.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Is the adjustment payment made to bondholders on reconversion subject to income tax?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this adjustment payment to bondholders on reconversion has an element of interest in it; that is, part of the payment involves interest which has accrued on the bond. Another part is entirely independent of the interest. In so far as the interest element is concerned, that is taxable in the hands of the holder of the bond, who in fact will be required when he surrenders the bond for conversion to sign an ownership certificate indicating the proportion of interest which has accrued thereon.
I may say that these ownership certificates are forwarded to the Department of National Revenue, so that all persons receiving this interest must report it in their income tax returns for the year 1958, the returns they will file next spring. The balance of the adjustment payment is not taxable; in other words it is tax free in the hands of the recipient.

Perhaps I should qualify that answer in one respect. What I said a moment ago applies to the ordinary holders of bonds throughout the country, but there may be cases where people deal exclusively in bonds, thereby earning an income therefrom, and these may be placed in a different category from that of the ordinary bondholders in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: DISCREPANCY IN FIGURES

On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister received from the municipal corporation of the united townships of Neelon and Garson a request to take immediate action to alleviate the present crisis in the nickel mining industry in northern Ontario where operations have been cut down to four days a week? If so, what action has been taken or is contemplated concerning this crucial problem?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Without notice it would be impossible to give a full answer to the question. In so far as the nickel industry is concerned, there has been a situation developing in the last year and a half or two years detrimental to the export of nickel. This was one of the matters which was discussed during the recent visit of the President of the United States.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I were to endeavour to answer all the speculative articles that appear I would be kept busy and have no time for anything else. that are made on me and all the speculative stories that are spoken about me, this shop might as well be closed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution, which has been recommended to the house by His Excellency:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the resumption of the British Columbia coast steamship service operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, including provisions for the appointment of an administrator to carry on all or any part of the said services, and for other related matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we do not intend to hold up this resolution, of course, but I should like to ask the Prime Minister two questions. The first relates to something he mentioned in his earlier statement but perhaps not in sufficient detail. When are we likely to get the bill if in fact the government wishes to proceed with its consideration tomorrow afternoon? Second, would the Minister of Labour do what I think the minister of labour did in 1950 on the occasion of the railway strike, and explain to the house in as much detail as possible what will be in the bill following the remarks of the Prime Minister. This was the procedure adopted in 1950.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
In so far as the bill is
concerned, Mr. Chairman, it will be available first thing tomorrow morning. It will be printed tonight. I could furnish the Leader of the Opposition as well as the representative of the C.C.F. with a mimeographed copy, and the bill itself will be printed this evening and made available tomorrow morning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask whether or not the bill will be in our boxes in the morning?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: That is the intention.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I thank the Prime Minister for his statement. It would be convenient for us if I could have a mimeographed copy of the bill any time this evening. I had a second question. Could the Minister of Labour add anything to what the Prime Minister has

already said this afternoon about the action the government proposes to take, and its form?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I do that may I refer to the fact that in speaking this afternoon on the proposal of the Prime Minister to introduce this resolution with the unanimous consent of the house, the Leader of the Opposition and also the hon. member for Skeena suggested that this government had not moved in this matter with sufficient speed, and had allowed a long period of time to elapse before finally deciding to take action. For the information of these hon. gentlemen I should like to briefly outline the history of this development. Probably in making their remarks this afternoon the hon. gentlemen lacked full knowledge of what has transpired throughout the course of this dispute.
On July 29, 1957, the Minister of Labour appointed a conciliation officer to mediate this dispute and meetings were held with representatives of the parties on August 1, 12, 13, 16 and 28. On August 30 the conciliation officer reported that he was not able to bring the parties to an amicable agreement and recommended the appointment of a conciliation board.
A conciliation board was appointed which sat for many days, heard the evidence and brought in three separate reports. The chairman recommended 25 per cent, the employee nominee recommended 31 per cent and the employer nominee recommended 17 per cent. This was rejected. The board conducted further negotiations on its own.
In the end we appointed a commissioner of inquiry, a man of high reputation for many years in these disputes, who spent close to five weeks presenting formulas of various kinds to both parties in order to bring about a settlement, but he failed in this. Eventually he recommended the form of arbitration. Immediately upon receiving his recommendation the Minister of Labour contacted all parties concerned to see if the recommendation was acceptable to them.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: You are referring to the commissioner from Toronto, whose name I have forgotten?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Mr. Taylor.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Eric Taylor.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
We received acquiescence from all the parties to proceed on the basis recommended by the commissioner of inquiry with the exception of the seafarers' international union, which rejected any form of arbitration. We then proceeded to call both parties
Canadian Pacific Steamships to Ottawa in the hope that I would be able to put forth some other formula that might be acceptable, and to afford an opportunity to the parties to present a formula that would be acceptable to the other party. Two meetings were held in Ottawa on July 7 and again on July 10. On July 10 we brought together the major principals of the dispute without any conclusion being reached.
Since those two meetings we have been in direct communication by telephone and other means with both parties, endeavouring to bring about some solution to this problem. I say this, Mr. Chairman, in order to inform the committee that every effort and indeed a continuous one has been made by the Department of Labour to bring about a solution.
As far as the bill is concerned and the request of the Leader of the Opposition for an outline of it, I think I will leave it to the Prime Minister, who has asked for the introduction of this bill, to outline its various aspects.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Can the minister tell us how many days these men have been out?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: They have been out since the strike began on May 16.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I understood the reading of the resolution correctly it contains three parts: first, the resumption of the services of the Pacific coast steamships; second, the appointment of an administrator; and third, other related matters. I wonder whether the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour could throw some light on these three parts of the resolution.
What I am directing my attention to at the moment is, in what form is it intended to suggest, direct or order the resumption of services? Next, what will be the duties of the administrator and what will be his functions? Will he have jurisdiction to get the parties together and will he be given a certain time in which to do that, or will there be no such time? Will the legislation resemble the legislation to which the Leader of the Opposition referred earlier? Finally, what are the other related matters that are mentioned in the legislation?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with
respect to the three phases of the matter referred to by the hon. member for Laurier, of which the first was the appointment of an administrator, the administrator is to be appointed by the governor in council to carry on all or any part of the business of the steamship company. He will be regarded as an agent of the steamship company for the purpose of carrying on its business. Forthwith upon his appointment he will carry on

Canadian Pacific Steamships the business of the steamship company which was suspended by reason of the strike, and every employee who is now on strike will be required to resume his duties or his employment with the steamship company.
As soon as the ships are put in operation there will be a direction that the steamship company and each union shall forthwith enter into negotiations with a view to settlement of any matters in dispute between them at the present time, and the authority of the administrator to carry on the business of the steamship company shall continue until a new collective agreement is concluded or until his appointment is terminated by the governor in council.
In order to secure the operation of the ships there will be a provision to the effect that the employees shall go back to work and that in general the negotiations shall continue with a view to determining, by the necessary operation of bargaining the questions still in dispute as between the S.I.U. particularly and the steamship company. I think that in general represents a summary.
There will, of course, have to be provision made for the assumption by the administrator of the full authority of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in operating the steamship company.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Is it contemplated to appoint an officer of the railway company to act as administrator?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: That has not been finally determined but is the subject of consideration. There are considerations on both sides, but I would feel that in general the administrator should be someone with considerable administrative business experience in a governmental sense, and also with knowledge of the problems of the operation of steamships and the like.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Under what authority is
this legislation being introduced?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I am not quite sure
what the hon. gentleman means.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
What I mean is this. By
virtue of what provision of the constitution in the legislation being introduced?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: It is because of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is involved, and it is a company under national jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I take it from what the
Prime Minister said that there will be a provision in this legislation requiring the employees to go back to work. What would happen in case they did not obey the direction of parliament? Is there a clause to cover that situation?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman
knows, there is general provision that any infraction of a statute passed by parliament is subject to a general penalty.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I ask
two questions which I think are pertinent. In view of the fact that the legislation proposed under this resolution does provide for compulsory operation of the ships my first question is, what is the basis under which the men would return to work, the contractual basis, wages, conditions, benefits, and all that sort of thing? My second question is, in view of the action which is proposed, was there any previous intimation given to the parties concerned that the government had the intention of introducing legislation of this kind?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
With respect to the
second question, may I say that during the negotiations every consideration had been given to bring about a determination of the unsatisfactory situation, and I think it was made very clear that unless some amicable agreement was arrived at it would be necessary for the parliament of Canada to act; that public security and maintenance of a proper regard for the rights of others would demand the introduction of such legislation.
I may say that in taking this course we are following the suggestion we made on August 30, 1950, when the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act was before the House of Commons and the leader of the Conservative party moved an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West, as follows:
That Bill No. 1 be not now read the second time but that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to a measure which would provide for the appointment of a national administrator to ensure immediate operation of the railways pending final solution of the dispute by the free process of collective bargaining.
It is consonant with the viewpoint thus expressed that we proceeded as we have in the resolution and as we intend to proceed in the bill.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister what action the government would propose to take if the free process of collective bargaining does not work out effectively under this administration of the steamship company. Under the 1950 procedure, if I remember correctly, provision was made to deal with an emergency under which operation of the railway could not be carried on. The particular contingency of a deadlock could not have arisen under the earlier legislation. May I ask the Prime Minister what the government proposes to do in case of a possible deadlock, if the administrator

is not able to operate the shipping company because the processes of collective bargaining have not worked out effectively?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
In 1950, of course, provision was made for compulsory arbitration under the legislation, and we opposed that at that time. On this occasion we simply make provision to get the men back to work and the ships in operation. If we get the ships in operation I believe we will have achieved the first major step. If other eventualities arise, and I am not here for the purpose of trying to envisage what the possibilities might be, then in that case, of course, we will be placed in a position where, if other action is necessary, it may be taken at that time.
The immediate purpose, the immediate aim and the immediate desire, I believe, not only of members of the house but generally is to bring about the restoration of the operation of these ships. Having done that, I feel that the negotiations that have been continuing will have renewed hopes of success.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
May I ask the
Minister of Labour, who was seized with these negotiations more directly, I suppose, than the Prime Minister, when it was intimated to the parties to the dispute that the government would give consideration to the course it is now following. When was that information given? Was it given as late as yesterday?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: During the discussions we did not give any intimation that any action would be taken, but we did point out that if the parties did not arrive at a solution themselves action would have to be taken to bring about the resumption of this vital service, because it is a public utility upon which so many people on Vancouver island depend. We did discuss certain aspects of the bill with the parties concerned yesterday.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Could the minister tell me when he did give information in the form in which he said it was given, a form which, if I understood the Prime Minister correctly, was not exactly as the Minister of Labour has just indicated?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: My question is, can the minister say when information was given as to possible action by the government?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: This particular action was discussed last night in all aspects with one of the parties interested.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I have been trying to get in on this discussion so perhaps between us
Canadian Pacific Steamships we may find the answers. With respect to the discussions between officials of the government or the Minister of Labour and one or both of the parties regarding the proposal to appoint an administrator to operate the ships, which proposal will be contained in the bill, were there any negotiations between either of the parties and the minister about the conditions surrounding the appointment of an administrator? In the event of the appointment of an administrator, did either of the parties indicate that this would be acceptable or not acceptable if certain other conditions were met? Was there any discussion of this nature? I am trying to determine whether, if the question was discussed, it was discussed at some length or expanded upon.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: We explored every avenue and had discussions with both parties about the possibilities of legislation at this time in order to see whether certain things were not acceptable for the purpose of resuming operations on the west coast. These discussions have been going on for several days now with one or other of the parties.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Discussions took place, but what I am trying to determine is whether there was an expansion or exploration of different ideas that would hinge upon the appointment of an administrator. Was there any discussion that centred around that sort of thing with one or both of the parties? Apparently the intent of the government was to find a solution mutually acceptable by each party to the dispute, which would probably be the most advantageous thing to do; but in attempting to reach mutual understanding or acceptability by the two parties was there any expansion on the idea of an administrator and any other matters discussed in relation to it?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Every aspect of the bill was discussed fully with both parties confidentially in the light of the desire on the part of the government to bring about a measure that would be acceptable to both sides to the dispute.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: May I ask one further question. The minister used the word "confidentially". Am I to take it from this that he is not able to discuss the trend or import of the discussions?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: We discussed every aspect of the bill that will be presented to parliament, but I do not feel that I can disclose the details or exact wording of our discussions.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
All right; we will let that one ride. There are one or two other questions I have in mind apart from the matter we have

Canadian Pacific Steamships just discussed. Has the government any particular person in mind? I realize that this question was answered to some extent a little while ago, but has the government any particular person in mind who might act as administrator?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Yes, the government has a person in mind, but no definite decision has been made that he will act in this capacity.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Has this individual been
approached and is it merely a question of awaiting his reply as to whether or not he will accept? Is that the hold-up?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I should like to look ahead a bit and ask the minister a question as to how this new operation, which we all hope will not have to be carried on for very long, is to be conducted. On what basis will the administrator get people to run his ships? What inducements will he oiler them in the way of wages, working conditions, other benefits and so on? If he has to offer them the salary scale and working conditions against which they are now striking, how is the administrator going to get these people back to work under the old conditions against which they have been striking now for four months? If the administrator offers better conditions, and he reaches the point where he has to offer the conditions which they have put forward as strikers and are asking for now, what will be the purpose in turning the shipping company over to the administrator?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: As I mentioned earlier, there has been an agreement signed between Canadian Pacific Steamships, west coast division, and the stewards union on the basis of an 8 per cent increase. The purpose of the bill is to provide for the resumption of work under the administrator by all employees on the same basis of an 8 per cent increase. All employees going back to work will have an increase of 8 per cent from the time the service is resumed.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: They go back to work, in other words, at a higher wage level than they had when they struck?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: May I ask the minister this. Is it true, as reported, that the Canadian Pacific has already disposed of two of their ten ships? Does the minister feel the Canadian Pacific has any obligation to maintain service between the mainland and Vancouver island if the strike is settled?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I have heard that the Canadian Pacific disposed of two of their ships.

My answer to the second part is that I feel they have an obligation.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: A legal obliga-gation?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I gather that this settlement is not to follow the same pattern as that which was followed by British Columbia with respect to the Black Ball ferries, that is in so far as the profit and loss picture of the company is concerned. The government or the treasury will not enter into any arrangement with the Canadian Pacific so far as taking the profits or making up the losses is concerned?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: No, it is not contemplated that the government should enter into that.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: A while ago the minister said it was the understanding between the company and the stewards that they would go back with an 8 per cent increase. Will the balance of the crew go back at that same rate? What was the demand of the union for the other members of the crew?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: There is a signed collective agreement, Mr. Chairman, between the Canadian Pacific and approximately 58 per cent of the employees in this service now on the basis of an 8 per cent increase. I am not able to say what the demands were. I can give the recommendations of the conciliation board. As I stated before, the chairman recommended a 25 per cent increase; the employer representative recommended a 17 per cent increase, and the employee representative recommended a 40 per cent or 50 per cent increase.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Perhaps the minister should explain that these 25 per cent and 17 per cent increases were divided into two amounts over a two-year period.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: That is true; it is a two-year contract, and part of it was for the first year and part of it for the second year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Earlier the minister referred to the two bargaining agencies involved, one the S.I.U. and the other the brotherhood of railway steamship clerks. In answer to a question put by the Leader of Opposition he said that the stewards, which I believe belong to the latter union, would go back to work at an 8 per cent increase. What is the position with respect to the other members of the other union, that is the S.I.U.? Do they go back at an increased wage?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I cannot say with certainty that they would go back, but I expect and have every hope that they will, at the same rate of 8 per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Is that contemplated in the bill?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: This is set out, that all the personnel go back at an 8 per cent increase.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Can the minister say what percentage of the men under contract belong to one union as opposed to the other?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: The average number of persons employed in this service on the west coast has been as follows: deck officers, represented by the Canadian merchant service guild, 62; engineering officers, represented by the national association of marine engineers, 93; unlicensed personnel represented by the S.I.U., 300; pursers and stewards, officers and ratings, represented by the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks, 413. This latter group is the one that has a collective agreement signed with the Canadian Pacific. The total average yearly employment with the company is approximately 930.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Thank you. May I go back to a question asked by someone earlier, I believe the hon. member for Essex East. What is the legal or constitutional position with regard to the company furnishing steamship service from the mainland to Vancouver island?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I do not quite follow what the hon. gentleman means.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I mean, for instance, with reference to the steamship service on the east coast from the mainland to Newfoundland, there is a constitutional obligation by virtue of the terms of union with Newfoundland. There is also an obligation with reference to steamship service on the west coast. I should like to know from the government what this is. Is it legal or constitutional or by virtue of what agreement between the provincial and federal governments, if such exists, that this steamship service be operated?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: It is not within my knowledge that there is any provision in the constitution or that there is an agreement that would cover the point mentioned by the hon. gentleman. The basis upon which we have jurisdiction is that the company is a company under federal jurisdiction. We are not asserting here any legislative jurisdiction by virtue of a written agreement, by virtue of a provision in the constitution for the provision of the service because, as I say, there is no such written or constitutional requirement. There is the fact that this company, and its service, is under the legislative jurisdiction of parliament.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
When the Leader of the Opposition asked the Minister of
Canadian Pacific Steamships Labour about two ships being disposed of by the company, and what was the minister's understanding as to the obligation of the company to carry on the operation with at least a limited number of ships, the Minister of Labour replied that he understood there was an obligation. I then put in an aside, was it a legal obligation? I do not expect the Minister of Labour to be able to answer whether or not there is a legal obligation, but perhaps he will explain what he meant by saying he understood there was an obligation as to the continuation of this service, which is so important?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: When I said there was an obligation I meant a moral obligation. After all, the Canadian Pacific have been operating these steamships for many years. People are dependent upon them, and they have more or less carried on the operation of this ferry service between the island and the mainland. After this bill is passed there certainly will be a legal obligation.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I am sure the Minister of Justice will give consideration to this. There must be a legal obligation on the part of the crown, in the right of Canada, to see that there is communication between the mainland and the island?

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: May I add to that question just one observation. Is there any obligation in the original franchise, if that is the right word, by which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was granted the right to build the transcontinental railroad? Is there any legal obligation in that franchise to continue the service to Vancouver island?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I believe that has been the subject of dispute and representation over the years. The fact is that the service was established. I would not care, at this stage, to revive a controversy which died many years ago. The fact is that the company has been providing a service. It is a company under the legislative jurisdiction of parliament, and it is on that basis that I would prefer to rest the authority for this legislation rather than enter into a hypothetical discussion as to whether or not there is now a legal or constitutional obligation on the company.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
The minister is aware, of course, that it was a condition of the union with British Columbia that a railway should be built to the pacific coast. Does the minister recall-I confess I do not-whether or not there was any obligation on the dominion at that time to provide steamship service between the mainland and Vancouver island?

Canadian Pacific Steamships

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:

It certainly has an immediate good effect of allowing the ships to go back into operation so that some sort of service is provided between Vancouver and Vancouver island, between Nanaimo and Vancouver, but it does practically nothing in respect of the over-all co-ordinated approach which must be taken by this government. I think the government has failed just as the previous administration failed, in not taking cognizance of and in not paying more attention to the shipping problems on the coast of British Columbia. I have mentioned this a number of times and will continue to do so, but these stop-gap measures-particularly this one in the light of its effect on the overall shipping on the coast of British Columbia-are merely short term approaches into which the government was jockeyed because it was unable to deal with the situation in past years.
We have always contended that if some sensible approach or attitude had been evident on the part of the previous administration and on the part of this administration with respect to the operating of shipping in this area we would probably not have got into this difficulty in the first place because, as hon. members will know, this difficulty arose because of a difference in opinion regarding the wage structure which would exist. I think if we analyse the matter, as did the junior chamber of commerce in Victoria, we will find that the fault lies with the Canadian Pacific steamship company more than it does with the union representing the employees.
Because of this difference of opinion, however, we ended up with a strike and I think we have to look at the attitude of the company which said "We cannot afford to pay any more than the 8 per cent which we signed

I am sure anyone who is familiar with the operation of the C.P.R. boats on the coast of British Columbia would not say that they are anything but inefficiently run, and that they are improperly built for that type of service.
All these factors have to be taken into consideration in looking at coastal shipping as a whole in British Columbia and I submit that while this legislation may have the immediate result of providing a service between one point and another out there, and of getting the employees back to work at a wage increase equal to that which the other employees got, there is no guarantee and, if you analyse the trend of collective bargaining and the attitudes taken and which could be taken in the future with respect to this particular strike, there is not even a pious hope that this will do anything more than have the immediate effect for which it is designed of getting these ships back into operation. This effect, of course, is a good thing because the general public is certainly suffering in British Columbia far more than anyone else, far more than the employees and far more than the company.
Unless and until the federal government which is in office now, and any other federal government which succeeds it is willing to take the final step of placing all coastal shipping in British Columbia under an allinclusive crown corporation, you are going to continue to have these problems you have now, you are going to have subsidies involved, and ships are going to lose money on some runs and make it on others, and then you will have to balance it up, and so on. Until you do that you are going to have problems of this kind arising because of the costs involved, and because of the wage rates, and because the attitude of the companies is that they cannot afford to pay anything better, while they have millions of dollars in other accounts and there is no argument about that.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting the resolution preceding this bill yesterday I outlined the general purpose of it and at this time I should like to briefly recapitulate some of the things which it is proposed to do by way of amendment to this bill. The general principle underlying the amendments which are proposed, of course, is to broaden the scope of the act and to thus make it possible to make payments to certain farmers and groups of farmers who heretofore have not been eligible for payments as the act is written at the present time. A very considerable number of farmers who have been precluded from receiving payment in the past because of the size of the minimum area which could be declared eligible for payment may now be put in receipt of payment and a considerable number of anomalies which have existed in the act will be removed by the amendments now proposed.
I should like to briefly outline the complaints and the proposed remedies and this will be a sort of brief compilation of what the amendments are and what their effect will be but before doing so I think I should point out to the house that it should be borne in mind that under legislation of this kind it is not feasible to pay awards to all farmers who suffer a crop loss in any particular year nor is it possible in all individual cases to make the award proportionate to each farmer's loss. This could be done only under a crop insurance scheme. We had a considerable amount of discussion yesterday with respect to a crop insurance scheme. The general opinion expressed by those who spoke on the resolution yesterday was that a crop insurance scheme should be brought into effect and I indicated that this was the opinion of the government and we were proceeding with that in mind.
However, this scheme has never been a crop insurance scheme. That was never the intention of this legislation. The main purpose of this act has always been to assist the municipalities and the provinces to deal with a relief problem which they could not otherwise undertake, or which they could not deal with alone, and I think that should be kept in mind in discussing the act, that this is not a crop insurance scheme. It has been, and essentially throughout the years has remained, a form of drought relief. That form of drought relief has been greatly extended to

cover other types of crop losses such as loss by rust, by grasshoppers, by hail and by flooding.
The majority of the complaints received- and they have been received, of course, for years-are protests against the inclusion of high-yield sections in an eligible area when computing the category of payment. It is proposed to exclude from both payment and the computations to determine the category of award all those sections having an average yield of 12 or more bushels; that is, the individual sections. This will enable the marking of payments on those sections with a loss of crop more in proportion to the loss.
Many complaints are also received from farmers in eligible townships who, even though they have a low yield, are excluded from payment because their lands are in a block of six or more sections with an average yield of over 10 bushels, that is contiguous to a high-yield township. It is proposed to repeal this section of the act and simply exclude xrom payment all sections having a yield of 12 or more bushels.
Many complaints are also received from farmers with a low yield who are in an ineligible township and denied an award because they do not form part of a block of six or more adjoining sections that is contiguous to an eligible township. It seems unfair to deny payments to such farmers when they are in many instances just across the road from an eligible township. It is therefore proposed to remove the restrictions as to the size of the block and make it possible to qualify any number of sections of land adjoining an eligible area, regardless of township boundaries as long as those sections are contiguous to one another.
It is also proposed to remove from the act the authority to exclude farmers with other occupations. It is felt that everyone who farms land himself, or hires the work done should participate in the benefits, particularly as the levy is collected from him.
Another proposal is to repeal that section of the act which excludes from award all crown lands which had not been sold or granted until after 1940. It is felt that farmers on such lands are as much entitled to an award as anyone else.
Many farmers complain that the minimum size of the area for eligibility, namely one-half of a township, that is, 18 sections, is too large. It is proposed to reduce this to one-third of a township, or 12 sections.
In areas where coarse grains are the predominant crop, many complain because wheat is used as the index in determining eligibility. They recommend the use of the predominant coarse grain crop. It is proposed to provide

Prairie Farm Assistance Act that the regulations may authorize the substitution of any grain for wheat where less than 10 per cent of the cultivated area is sown to wheat. That 10 per cent figure was taken because in any township where 10 per cent or more of the land is sown to wheat in nearly all cases that 10 per cent will perhaps be the best land, the land which has been summerfallowed and so forth, and therefore if the yield on that land is low the yield on the other land is likely to be considerably lower. Therefore, continuing to use wheat as the index in cases where more than 10 per cent of the township is planted to wheat means that the farmer will get a better deal than if you take merely the predominant coarse grain crop. In other words, where you had 15 per cent of the township planted in wheat, 45 per cent of it planted in oats and 30 per cent planted in barley, if you took in that case oats the farmers in most cases would not get as good a payment as if you took the wheat as an index for payment.
Many farmers also feel that crops other than wheat, oats barley and rye, should be subject to the one per cent levy deducted at the elevators. Since flax and rapeseed are now grown in large quantity it is proposed to make these subject to the levy also. The growers of these benefit under the act in a year of crop failure and have benefited, of course, for many years past, and it seems unfair when they benefit that they should not contribute toward the fund the same as the growers of wheat, oats, barley and rye.
Some complaints come from farmers who suffer from flooding because they feel that the minimum area to qualify is too large.

One of the major amendments to the regulations will be to qualify for payment lands operated by Indians within reservations. The hon. member for Essex East asked about this yesterday and I gave him a guarantee. In future such lands will come under the operations of the act on the same basis as other lands.
I think this summary I have given of the various amendments covers all of those which are of any considerable importance and I would hope that all of them would receive the unanimous approval of the house.

speechtext:
The reason for the amendment is that in recent years an increasing number of families operating farms have organized themselves as family corporations

Such corporations have been ineligible to receive awards under the act as it stood and therefore we are including family corporations of that kind in the definition of "farmer" so that these people will be eligible for awards in the future. speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-41, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act at the resolution stage, I stated that it has two purposes. One is to permit payment of compensation at market value for cattle ordered slaughtered in controlling an outbreak of a serious animal disease which was not normally present in Canada. The other is to raise the statutory maximum compensation rates for cattle ordered slaughtered in connection with area or herd eradication programs for such diseases as tuberculosis and brucellosis.
Section 11 of the act authorizes the minister to order the slaughter of animals suffering from or exposed to an infectious or contagious disease. Subsection (1) of section 12 authorizes him to order compensation to be paid to the owners of such animals, and subsection (2) of that section establishes the basis of compensation.
If members will turn to the explanatory note accompanying the bill they will find there the present wording of subsection (2) of section 12. It will be noted that the authorized compensation is the market value of the animal except in the instance of horses and cattle, for which maximum compensation amounts are specified by paragraphs (a) and (b).
The amendment, which is to paragraph (b), limits the exception in the case of cattle to those ordered slaughtered pursuant to any area or herd disease eradication program. The effect of this will be to permit payment of compensation at market value in such circumstances as the foot-and-mouth outbreak in 1952. While such circumstances are rare, I am sure the house would agree that in those instances the owners of cattle which are ordered slaughtered in the national interest should receive full compensation for them.
The most important impact of the amendment will be in relation to compensation paid under the tuberculosis and brucellosis 57071-3-164
23, 1958
Animal Contagious Diseases Act eradication programs. At the present time the maximum compensation is $100 for purebred animals and $40 for grade animals. The amendment will increase those maximum figures to $140 for purebreds and $70 for grades. It may help in an understanding of the bill to explain briefly the nature of those programs.
The restricted area plan for tuberculosis was introduced in 1922. Areas are established, usually counties in eastern Canada and municipalities in western Canada, on the recommendation of a provincial minister of agriculture and following a request to him by a majority of the cattle owners in the area. All the cattle in the area are then tested for tuberculosis, reactors are removed from herds and if the incidence of tuberculosis is below one-half of one per cent the area is accredited. There is also an individual herd plan, known as the accredited herd plan, which operates on a somewhat more stringent basis and which is also entered into voluntarily by herd owners.
All sections of all provinces are now included in tuberculosis restricted areas. The programs have virtually eliminated tuberculosis from Canadian cattle herds. As an illustration of that, the incidence of tuberculosis in cattle tested has declined from four per cent at the start of the program to only slighly over one-tenth of one per cent last year.
A similar program for the eradication of brucellosis, or Bang's disease, was introduced in 1957. It operates on virtually the same basis as the area plan for tuberculosis. Most provinces have now requested the establishment of some brucellosis control areas, and the testing has been under way for some months.
In these programs it has never been considered necessary nor, in fact, desirable to compensate owners of reacting animals at their full market value. When an animal reacts to the test the owner is required to dispose of it for slaughter, under post mortem examination, and receives the carcass value of the animal. Also, the removal of reacting animals from the herd is to the owner's advantage as well as in the national interest. For these reasons the act has always placed a maximum limitation on the amount of compensation which can be paid for cattle and this principle is maintained in the present amendment in so far as programs of this nature are concerned.
The maximum compensations now authorized by the act, $100 for purebreds and $40 for grades, have been in effect since 1923. There have been numerous representations to the government from farm and livestock

Animal Contagious Diseases Act organizations that these rates are no longer equitable in relation to present cattle values. We have felt that these representations are valid and propose, by the present bill, to increase the maximum compensations to $140 for purebred cattle and $70 for grades.
I should perhaps explain the implication of the last portion of section 1 of the bill which reads:
-and if the sale of the carcass is unlawful an additional amount for purebred and grade animals equal to the value the carcass would have if the sale were lawful.
I mentioned earlier that if an animal is ordered to be slaughtered under the tuberculosis or brucellosis eradication programs the owner is required to dispose of it for slaughter and receives the slaughter value. All such animals are directed to plants operating under federal meat inspection, where they are subjected to veterinary post-mortem examination. When the infection is limited, the infected portions are condemned and the balance of the carcass is eligible for sale.
The effect of the last part of section 1 is that if the infection is sufficiently general as to require the entire carcass to be condemned an additional compensation may be paid to the owner to the value the carcass would have had if it had not been condemned. This provision has been in the act for some time.
Members will note from section 2 of the bill that the amended compensation rates will become effective on April 1, 1958. As I stated earlier we have just recently started testing under the new brucellosis area program. When we accept an area under the program on the recommendation of a province and start testing the cattle in it, our veterinarians move progressively from farm to farm. The owner does not have the privilege of electing when he will have his herd tested. Some, therefore, are tested at the beginning of the operation and some at the end.
We felt that it would be inequitable to have circumstances where some owners who quite fortuitously did not have their cattle tested until after the enactment of this bill may receive a higher rate of compensation than their neighbours who may have had their herds tested a few days before that. It was felt, therefore, that the amended rates should be effective from the first of the fiscal year which also coincides with the beginning of the main activity in brucellosis testing.
I might say that I had representations from a considerable number of hon. members in connection with the last point I mentioned of setting the date when the act will become effective and particularly from the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). It seemed to
[Mr. Harkness.l
me it was only the reasonable thing to do although in general I must say I am very much opposed to retroactive legislation of any sort. But in view of the fact that the program has just started and for the other reasons I mention about inequities that would occur if the date of enforcement were not set back to the beginning of the fiscal year and the beginning of the testing program the April date has been put in the act.
I have gone into these tuberculosis and brucellosis schemes as well as into other matters in some detail because I find there has been and there remains a considerable amount of misapprehension in regard to what the Animal Contagious Diseases Act provides for and the reasons for which compensation is paid for animals ordered to be slaughtered. As I indicated in answer to a question yesterday, the act does not provide compensation for animals which die of a particular disease. It provides for compensation only for animals which are ordered to be slaughtered when it is felt in the national interest they should be slaughtered in order to prevent the spread of a disease.

To do so, the farmers formed various agricultural organizations, study groups and particularly what is known as the famous milk control which is now the subject of disputes and debates in Montreal and in my riding. The milk producers realized that in their own interest they had to protect themselves against milk distributors in Montreal, and, to that end, they established what is called a zone. This step was of the utmost importance for them but at the same time could entail serious consequences.

Mr. Speaker, anyone who has had anything to do with the production of livestock throughout the years realizes the excellent work that is being done by those who have had the authority to administer this act across Canada. In my opinion the administration has been continually improved and has brought about a great deal of advantage to farmers and producers of livestock and consumers of their products. I was pleased to note in this amending bill that the government is giving favourable response to representations of various organizations which are concerned with this matter. While the bill in one respect might be considered a piece of minor legislation, it is of great importance to the agricultural industry as a whole. We in this group intend to support the measure.
However, I do want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the administration of the act and the requirement that the farmer or the cattle producer must have his cattle slaughtered in a licensed packinghouse places some of those farmers and cattle producers at a considerable extra expense. For instance, Mr. Speaker, in my constituency I think in order to reach a licensed slaughter house operating under the regulations that are required under this act the farmer would

For some who have cattle in the Lardeau valley, in the Beaver lake district and in the Pend d'Oreille this is a considerable extra expense; so much so that under normal circumstances I would say it would not be worth the farmer's while to truck a few cattle this long distance over rough mountain roads. my attention. In any event, ordinarily cattle going in would be shipped along with other cattle going for slaughter also. I know that the area from which the hon. member comes is in a somewhat isolated valley in British Columbia in which there is no railway transportation and where water transportation has been very seriously curtailed in recent years and therefore the transportation problem for cattle, as well as for most other things, is a rather serious one. I sympathize with him as far as that situation is concerned but it is not a problem which has been brought to my attention before or over which there has been any complaint.

speechtext: I have only one question to ask the minister. I wish to remind him of what I said yesterday. I said that the amounts of $140 for purebred cows and $70 for grade cows were not enough. Would the minister explain how the figures of $140 and $70 were arrived at?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
As far as grade animals are concerned, in the majority of cases where an animal is ordered slaughtered $70 plus the value of the carcass would give a pretty good return. In some cases the return would be higher than the market value of the animal.
With respect to purebreds, as the hon. member knows, some purebred animals run up to many thousands of dollars apiece and I think it is not a practical proposition to ask us to determine what the particular value is in the case of such animals. If you pay compensation at the rate of $140 a head, that amount plus the value of the carcass brings you pretty close to the average value of most purebred animals. If it is a particularly good animal that is not so but, as I say, if we were to try to determine what the value of a particularly good cow was it would lead us into all sorts of difficulties.
The hon. member was not here something over a year ago when, as the hon. member for Essex East will remember, we had a great deal of difficulty over determining the value of sheep. An inquiry was made by the agricultural committee as a result of charges made by one or two members of the house, which charges were not vindicated by the committee. Nevertheless, this has been something that has caused trouble for some years past and a great deal of talk which was not justified. If we had to do this in the case of every cow slaughtered under the brucellosis and tuberculosis testing programs we would really be faced with an impossible problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would reply to a few questions concerning the matter which came up earlier, one Walter Mitchell. I do not propose to debate it at any length in view of the shortness of time, but perhaps the minister would tell me, first of all, upon whose recommendation Mr. Mitchell was dismissed because of political partisanship.

As I indicated in answer to the hon. gentleman's starred question this afternoon, it was on my recommendation and order. When I had placed before me all the circumstances concerning this case, which I outlined very briefly this afternoon, it seemed to me there was no question whatever but that I had no option except to dismiss this man. As I indicated, he had been securing contraband goods from the ships which he had been inspecting as an inspector of the department, and this puts the department in an extremely bad position to have things of that sort occurring. I think there is no question at all but that the man had to be dismissed. As soon as I learned of this, I did dismiss him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it that there were two reasons for dismissal, first, the political reason, and I take it that it was on the recommendation of the minister, and the second the possession of contraband liquor and cigarettes, as the minister stated. speechtext: May I ask the minister, then, if any prosecution was instituted against this man because of the charge the minister made this afternoon?

speechtext: May I inquire from the minister as to whether or not this man is a casual employee who works during the navigation season, that is from the opening of navigation in April until the closing of navigation in December?

speechtext: The information about the possession of contraband liquor came to the attention of the minister, according to his statement this afternoon, on November 29?

speechtext: If this contraband liquor was in his possession on November 29, can the minister say whether or not he was still a casual employee performing his duties or whether he had ceased his casual work? Was it during the navigation season?

speechtext: The minister says the information did not come to his attention until considerably later, I think he said about two months ago?

speechtext: I am not going to hold the minister down to dates, I can assure him about that immediately. But I should like to get as much information as I can, as accurately as I can.
